771.title: The happy sleeper
771.hook: Hatthaka asks the Buddha if he slept well on the frozen ground; yes, better than anyone (AN 3.34)
771.howItsDone: Monks and nuns in the forest traditions sometimes sleep simply, on a mat or the ground, and some Buddhists recall the Buddha's posture of lying on the right side, mindful, as they go to sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gahapati, a householder answering the elders with two oxen and one yoke. Your line: a householder teaches. Today, a cold night outdoors.

Frost on the ground. Leaves sparse on the trees. A cold wind blowing. That's the winter night the Anguttara describes, near the town of Alavi. In the morning a man named Hatthaka, out walking, finds the Buddha beside a cattle track, sitting on a thin spread of leaves. So Hatthaka asks what anyone asks a guest in the morning: did you sleep well? Yes, the Buddha says. I'm one of those in the world who sleep well. Hatthaka can hardly believe it.
screen: `FROST AND A COLD WIND.` → `DID YOU SLEEP WELL?` → `YES.`

segments.voice: First, the doubt. Hatthaka lists it all back: cold winter nights, ground trampled hard by cattle hooves, a thin spread of leaves, thin robes, a cold wind. How could anyone sleep well out here? Second, the counter-question. Let me ask you something, the Buddha says, and answer as you like. Take a householder with a fine house, plastered inside and out, closed against the wind, its door bolted and its windows shut. A couch spread with long-fleeced woolen covers. A lamp burning. People attending him. Would he sleep well? Yes, says Hatthaka. Third, the turn. And if a fever of lust arose in him, or hatred, or delusion, burning in body and mind, would he sleep badly? Yes, he would. Fourth, the end of the fever. Those burnings, the very things that keep the comfortable man awake, the Buddha says, have been abandoned in him, cut off at the root like a palm stump that can't grow again. So he sleeps well, even on frozen leaves. The discourse ends in a verse: the one who is fully at peace sleeps at ease, cooled, with nothing left to burn. It isn't a teaching against beds, or houses, or blankets. It's a question about what actually keeps a person awake. I sleep well.
screen: `COLD GROUND, THIN LEAVES.` · `A RICH MAN'S WARM HOUSE.` · `THE FEVER THAT KEEPS HIM UP.` · `CUT OFF LIKE A PALM STUMP.` · then, large: `I SLEEP WELL.`

segments.voice: Ask Hatthaka's question of your own nights: what actually keeps me up? Maybe not the mattress; maybe a worry, a grudge, the pull of one more scroll, and if something comes, name it gently, without trying to fix it. Then let a few slow breaths go out, the way they might once your head is on the pillow.
Sukha, ease. What the Buddha says he sleeps in, even on frozen ground, because nothing in him is left burning. Today's word.
Your line: I sleep well. Ease, here, has more to do with the mind than the bed. Rest well.

772.title: Culapanthaka's white cloth
772.hook: a slow monk rubs a white cloth until it's gray and understands (Dhammapada 25 story)
772.howItsDone: Teachers in Buddhist communities retell Culapanthaka's story to encourage students who learn slowly, and in some monasteries cleaning and sweeping are themselves treated as mindfulness practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sukha, ease on frozen leaves, with nothing left burning. Your line: I sleep well. Today, a monk who couldn't learn one verse.

One verse. That's all the young monk Culapanthaka has to learn, and it won't stay. The Dhammapada commentary tells how he tries and tries, and every new line pushes out the one before. His older brother, Mahapanthaka, an accomplished monk, finally gives up on him and tells him to go home. So early one morning Culapanthaka stands at the monastery gate, in tears, ready to leave. The Buddha meets him there, takes him by the hand, and leads him back inside. Today, what the Buddha hands him.
screen: `ONE VERSE WON'T STAY.` → `GO HOME, SAYS HIS BROTHER.` → `THE BUDDHA AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: First, the cloth. Not another verse. The Buddha gives him a clean white cloth, and tells him to sit and rub it with his hand, repeating a short phrase: removing dirt, removing dirt. Second, the change. As he rubs, the clean cloth slowly grows soiled. The commentary says he saw it plainly: this cloth was pure white, and now, because of this body, it's dirty. Things change. Third, the inner cloth. Then the Buddha speaks to him about the real dirt: not dust, but greed, hatred and delusion. Those are what a monk removes. The commentary says Culapanthaka understood, right there, and became an arahant. Fourth, the meal. That same day, the story goes on, the physician Jivaka, the doctor of three days ago, had invited the Buddha and the monks to his house. Mahapanthaka, who arranged the invitations, had left his slow brother out. The Buddha wouldn't begin until Culapanthaka was sent for. And the commentary attaches a Dhammapada verse to his story: by rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and self-control, the wise one makes an island no flood can sweep away. The slow monk didn't get there by memorizing. He got there with a cloth, his own two hands, and a teacher who met him at the gate. The cloth grows gray.
screen: `A WHITE CLOTH, NOT A VERSE.` · `THE CLEAN CLOTH GROWS SOILED.` · `THE REAL DIRT IS INSIDE.` · `SENT FOR, AT JIVAKA'S MEAL.` · then, large: `THE CLOTH GROWS GRAY.`

segments.voice: If there's a cloth nearby, a napkin, a dish towel, a sleeve, take it in your hands; if not, use the hem of your shirt. Rub it slowly between your fingers, feel the weave, and notice that your hands are already leaving something on it: warmth, a little oil, a crease. Nothing stays exactly as it was.
Rajoharana, removing dirt. The phrase the Buddha gave Culapanthaka to repeat while rubbing a clean cloth until it was soiled. Today's word.
Your line: the cloth grows gray. Slow to memorize didn't mean slow to see. Until tomorrow.

773.title: Sunita the flower-scavenger
773.hook: a man of the lowest caste, sweeping discarded flowers, is invited to ordain (Theragatha, Sunita)
773.howItsDone: Teachers retell Sunita's story when speaking of the Buddha's welcome to people of every background, and Sunita's verses are read as part of the Theragatha, the collection of poems by the early elder monks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rajoharana, a clean cloth slowly soiled in a slow monk's hands. Your line: the cloth grows gray. Today, a man who carried away dead flowers.

Born in a low family. Poor. Little to eat. That's how Sunita describes himself in his verses in the Theragatha, the poems of the elder monks. His work was lowly too, he says: he carried away withered flowers, the ones people had thrown out. People despised him and looked down on him, and he kept his mind humble and bowed to many. Then one day he saw the Buddha walking into the chief city of Magadha, with the company of monks around him. Today, what happened on that street.
screen: `POOR, AND LITTLE TO EAT.` → `CARRYING AWAY DEAD FLOWERS.` → `THE BUDDHA ON THE STREET.`

segments.voice: First, the pole. Sunita sets down his carrying pole and goes to pay his respects. And in his verse, the Buddha, the highest of men, stops and stands still, out of compassion for him. Second, the question. Sunita bows at the Teacher's feet, stands to one side, and asks to go forth, to become a monk. Third, the answer. The Buddha, compassionate toward the whole world, says, come, monk. And Sunita says: that was my ordination. Two words, spoken on a street, to a man whose job was clearing away other people's dead flowers. Fourth, the end of the poem. He goes off alone into the forest and practices as the Teacher taught him, and the verses say he reached the end of the path. Then the gods come and honor him with joined palms, and the Buddha smiles and speaks a verse: by austerity, by the holy life, by restraint and taming, this is how one becomes a brahmin; this is the highest brahminhood. The word brahmin is still there, but in the Buddha's mouth it's about how someone lives, not the family they were born to. The man people stepped around becomes the one the gods bow to. And the first thing that happened to him wasn't a test. It was a welcome. The sweeper was welcome.
screen: `HE PUTS DOWN HIS POLE.` · `MAY I GO FORTH?` · `COME, MONK.` · `HONORED BY HOW HE LIVES.` · then, large: `THE SWEEPER WAS WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Picture the people your days pass by without a word: whoever empties the bins at work, cleans the restroom, drops off the delivery. Choose one face, or one role, and hold them in mind for a few breaths, the way the Buddha stopped on the street. Let a plain wish for their well-being come.
Sunita. The poor flower-scavenger, despised for his low birth, whom the Buddha stopped for and welcomed with two words: come, monk.
Your line: the sweeper was welcome. Honor, in that verse, comes from how a person lives. That's day seven hundred seventy-three.

774.title: Sopaka's cremation ground
774.hook: a boy abandoned in a charnel ground is found by the Buddha (Theragatha, Sopaka)
774.howItsDone: In Theravada countries children can be ordained as novices, and the short set of novice's questions linked to Sopaka is chanted and learned in monasteries as part of the Khuddakapatha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sunita, the flower-scavenger welcomed on the street with two words. Your line: the sweeper was welcome. Today, a boy alone in the dark.

A cremation ground at night is no place for anyone, least of all a child. The commentaries on the elder monks' verses tell two stories under the name Sopaka, and they don't match. In one, a relative who was angry with a boy took him there, tied him down beside a body, and left. In the other, a boy was born there, after his mother was taken for dead. Some scholars think these are two different monks who shared a name. In both, the Buddha comes to the child. Today, the boy who was found.
screen: `A CREMATION GROUND AT NIGHT.` → `A BOY LEFT ALONE.` → `THE BUDDHA SEES HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. In the telling with the relative, the boy, bound and afraid, calls out in the dark. The Buddha, far away, sees him, and the story says light reaches him, the bonds fall away, and he's brought to the Buddha. The tradition tells it as a wonder, and it's told that way here. Second, the verses. In the Theragatha, the lines under the name Sopaka are quieter. He saw the Buddha walking in the shade of a building, he says. He went up, arranged his robe over one shoulder, bowed, and walked behind him. Third, the questions. Then the Buddha asks him questions, and Sopaka answers without fear. The Buddha is pleased, and with a few words of welcome, receives him into the order. Later tradition connects him with a short set of questions and answers for a young novice, which begins: what is one? All beings live by food. Fourth, what the story keeps doing. The details shift from telling to telling, but the shape holds. A child left alone in the dark is seen. He's not lectured. He's asked questions, and listened to, and his answers are taken seriously. He's given a place, a teacher, and a community to belong to. The cremation ground is where his story begins, not where it ends. Found.
screen: `A CRY IN THE DARK.` · `WALKING BEHIND THE BUDDHA.` · `QUESTIONS, ANSWERED WITHOUT FEAR.` · `SEEN, HEARD, GIVEN A PLACE.` · then, large: `FOUND.`

segments.voice: Hold one child in mind: in your family, on your street, at a school you know, or the child you once were. Ask one plain question: what would help them be a little safer, a little more heard? If nothing comes, simply wish them well, and let the question rest.
Susana, a cremation ground. Where a boy left alone at night was found, questioned kindly, and welcomed by the Buddha. Today's word.

775.title: Mahakaccana the explainer
775.hook: the disciple who unfolds short teachings in detail (MN 18)
775.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes take a short saying of the Buddha and explain it at length in a talk, and the Honey Ball discourse is studied for its step-by-step account of how perception turns into proliferating thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday: susana, the cremation ground where the boy Sopaka was found, questioned kindly and welcomed. Your line: found. Today, a monk who answers by unfolding.

A man leaning on his walking stick asks the Buddha a blunt question. His name is Dandapani, a Sakyan out for a stroll, and in the Middle Length Discourses he asks: what does the ascetic teach? What does he proclaim? The Buddha gives a short, strange answer. Dandapani shakes his head, raises his eyebrows, and walks off, still leaning on his stick. That evening the Buddha tells the monks about it. One monk asks what he meant, and the Buddha answers with another short saying, gets up, and goes inside. And the monks look at each other.
screen: `A MAN WITH A STICK.` → `A SHORT, STRANGE ANSWER.` → `THE MONKS ARE PUZZLED.`

segments.voice: First, the short saying. Roughly: when a person finds nothing in the world to delight in, to welcome, or to cling to, that is the end of the hidden tendencies of the mind, and the end of taking up sticks and weapons, of quarrels and fights. Then the Buddha went in. Second, the go-to monk. The monks remember that the Teacher praised Mahakaccana as able to explain at length what was said in brief. So they go to him. He chides them, gently: you had the Teacher himself, and you came to me, like someone who wants heartwood and walks past the root and the trunk to search among the branches. Then he unfolds it anyway. Third, the unfolding. Eye and form meet, and seeing arises. The three together are contact. With contact comes feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. And what one thinks about, one spins out, on and on, until the spinning comes back and besets the person who started it. That's the road to the quarrels. Fourth, the seal. The monks take it back to the Buddha, who says: Mahakaccana is wise. If you had asked me, I would have explained it the same way. Ananda says it's like a hungry, tired man who finds a honey cake: wherever he tastes it, it's sweet. So the Buddha gives the discourse a name: the Honey Ball. Unfold it.
screen: `NOTHING TO CLING TO.` · `GO ASK MAHAKACCANA.` · `CONTACT, FEELING, THINKING, SPINNING.` · `THE HONEY BALL.` · then, large: `UNFOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Take one short thing you say often that others don't quite get: a rule at home, a phrase at work, something you know so well you've stopped explaining it. Walk through it step by step in your mind, the way Mahakaccana did, this, then this, then this, and notice each step you usually skip.
Madhupindika, the honey ball. The name given to the discourse where Mahakaccana unfolded the Buddha's short saying step by step. Today's word.
Your line: unfold it. A short saying can hold a long road. Day seven hundred seventy-five, done.

776.title: Devadatta
776.hook: the cousin who wanted to lead the order
776.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell Devadatta's story as a warning about gain, honor and ambition inside a spiritual community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: madhupindika, the Honey Ball, a short saying unfolded step by step. Your line: unfold it. Today, the start of a cautionary tale: a monk who wanted to be in charge.

The Vinaya puts Devadatta in good company. A group of young Sakyan nobles leave home together to follow the Buddha: Anuruddha, Ananda, Bhaddiya and others, with the barber Upali alongside. Devadatta is one of them. Tradition remembers him as the Buddha's cousin. For a while his story runs like theirs. Then, the text says, he starts to wonder whom he could win over, someone whose favor would bring him gain and honor. He chooses a prince, Ajatasattu, the king's son. Today, what Devadatta wanted next.
screen: `YOUNG NOBLES LEAVE HOME.` → `DEVADATTA AMONG THEM.` → `WHOM CAN I WIN OVER?`

segments.voice: First, the patron. Devadatta impresses the young prince with a show of power, and the prince begins sending him food, morning and evening, in carts. Gain and honor pour in. Second, the request. Then Devadatta goes to the Buddha, in front of a large gathering, and says: you're old now, Lord. Live at ease. Hand the order of monks over to me, and I'll lead it. Third, the refusal. The Buddha says no. I wouldn't hand the order over even to Sariputta and Moggallana, he says, let alone to you. The words are sharp, and spoken in public. The text says Devadatta left angry and displeased, and that this was the first grudge he held against the Buddha. Fourth, the warning. Elsewhere in the canon the Buddha says gain, honor and praise came to Devadatta for his own ruin, the way a banana plant bears fruit and then dies, or a bamboo or a reed fruits and is finished. In the story, the trouble isn't leading itself: other disciples taught, guided and looked after the monks. What the text holds up is the wish to take charge, fed by carts of food and a prince's favor. That's where Devadatta's story turns. The wish to lead.
screen: `A PRINCE'S FAVOR.` · `HAND THE ORDER TO ME.` · `NOT EVEN TO SARIPUTTA.` · `FRUIT THAT KILLS THE PLANT.` · then, large: `THE WISH TO LEAD.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day or two for a moment when you wanted the final say, in a meeting, a group chat, at home. That's ordinary; now look closer at what fed it, getting things right, helping people, or being seen as the one, and there may be some of each. Don't judge it; just name it, and let the breath carry on.
Devadatta. A Sakyan monk, remembered as the Buddha's cousin, who grew rich in gain and honor and asked to be handed the order. Today's word.
Your line: the wish to lead. Gain and honor came first; the grudge came after. Until tomorrow.

777.title: Devadatta's plots
777.hook: the boulder rolled down, the elephant sent, the split in the community (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)
777.howItsDone: Teachers in Theravada communities tell Devadatta's plots from the Vinaya as a warning about envy and ambition, and the scene of the elephant Nalagiri calmed by loving-kindness appears in Buddhist art and in retellings of the Buddha's life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devadatta, the cousin who asked to lead the order and was refused. Your line was the wish to lead. Today, what that wish turned into.

A slope below Vulture's Peak, outside Rajagaha. The Buddha is walking in the shade of the hill. Up on the ridge, a man shoves a large rock over the edge. The Vinaya says the rock was stopped before it reached him, but a splinter broke off, struck the Buddha's foot, and drew blood. The man on the ridge is Devadatta. The Cullavagga tells his story as a chain: hired men on a road, a falling rock, an elephant set loose, and last, the one the text slows down for.
screen: `A ROCK FROM VULTURE'S PEAK.` → `A SPLINTER, AND BLOOD.` → `A CHAIN OF PLOTS.`

segments.voice: First, the hired men. In the Vinaya's telling, Devadatta sends men to kill the Buddha on a road. One by one they arrive, lose their nerve, sit down, and hear him teach. They go home as followers. Second, the rock, which Devadatta tries himself. Afterward, the Vinaya has the Buddha tell his monks that no one can take a Tathagata's life by violence. Third, the elephant. Devadatta gets the keepers to turn Nalagiri, a fierce elephant, loose on the road where the Buddha walks for alms. People scatter. The Buddha meets him with loving-kindness, metta, and the text says the elephant lowers his trunk, takes dust from the Buddha's feet, scatters it on his own head, and backs away. Fourth, the split, and here the story changes key. Devadatta goes after the community. He proposes five strict rules: live in the forest, eat only alms food, wear only rag robes, sleep under trees, eat no fish or meat. They sound devout. The Buddha answers that any monk who wishes may keep them, but he won't make them binding on all. Devadatta says this proves the Buddha has gone soft, gathers newly ordained monks, and leads them away to Gayasisa. The Buddha had already warned him that splitting the sangha is a grave thing, and tradition says it is one of the deeds that bring the heaviest results. But the chapter doesn't end with the split. Sariputta and Moggallana walk to Gayasisa, teach the young monks, and bring them home.
screen: `HIRED MEN WHO SAT DOWN TO LISTEN.` · `THE ROCK, AND THE SPLINTER.` · `NALAGIRI LOWERS HIS TRUNK.` · `FIVE RULES, AND A SPLIT.` · then, large: `THE SPLIT.`

segments.voice: Let one small split come to mind: two friends who stopped talking, a family thread gone quiet, a coworker you've been routing around. See where you stand in it, and look for one small step back across the line, a question or a plain hello. You don't have to take it yet; just find it, and hold it while the breath moves.
Devadatta's plots. Hired men, a rock, a fierce elephant, and finally a split in the sangha, the one the Buddha called grave. Today's word.
Your line: the split. A rock wounds a foot; a split wounds the thing that carries the teaching forward. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: Devadatta asks the Buddha to make five strict rules binding on every monk: forest, alms food only, rag robes, sleeping under trees, no fish or meat. what does the Buddha say?
options: make them binding on everyone.
let anyone who wishes keep them, but require none.
forbid them outright.
fork.reveal: he leaves them open to anyone who wishes and refuses to require them. Devadatta uses the refusal to split the community.

original.note: Pali saṅghabheda: a split in the sangha, the community of monks and nuns.

trapdoor: what you thought: a villain who tried to kill the Buddha.
what it means: the attacks on his body fail one by one; the plot the story weighs most is the split in the community.
what a scholar hears: the plots are told in the Cullavagga's chapter on splitting the sangha, so the whole story sits inside the rules for what counts as a schism.

chat.says: Why does the story treat Devadatta's split as worse than the rock?
options: A rock wounds a foot; a split wounds the community that carries the teaching.
Because the rock missed, so it never really counted as an attack.
Because the five rules he proposed were wrong for any monk to keep.
chat.meaning: The Buddha warned that splitting the sangha is grave: a rock wounds one foot, but a split wounds what carries the teaching forward.
